title: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
ref: NCERT Chemistry Part I · Unit 1 · pp. 1–28
note: Question text is taken from published copies of each year's paper. Question numbers differ between booklet codes, so only the year is shown. Every answer was worked out independently; 2021 is also checked against NTA's final answer key.

questions.q: Dalton's Atomic theory could not explain which of the following?
questions.sol:
Dalton's postulates (indivisible atoms, fixed whole-number ratios, atoms neither created nor destroyed) account for the three mass laws: conservation of mass, definite proportions and multiple proportions.

They cannot explain Gay-Lussac's law of gaseous volumes. Two volumes of H₂ and one volume of O₂ give two volumes of water vapour, which needs molecules that split into atoms. Avogadro later explained this; Dalton's model did not.
questions.hint: NCERT says it directly at the end of §1.5.

questions.check: Matches the published Code AA key
questions.q: In which case is the number of molecules of water maximum?
o: 0.00224 L of water vapours at 1 atm and 273 K
questions.sol:
Number of molecules ∝ number of moles, so convert each option to moles:

  • 0.00224 L ÷ 22.4 L mol⁻¹ = 10⁻⁴ mol
  • 0.18 g ÷ 18 g mol⁻¹ = 10⁻² mol
  • 18 mL of liquid water ≈ 18 g (density ≈ 1 g mL⁻¹) = 1 mol
  • 10⁻³ mol

18 mL of water holds 1 mol, i.e. NA molecules: the largest.
questions.hint: Turn every quantity into moles first.

questions.q: Which one of the followings has maximum number of atoms?
o: 1 g of O<sub>2</sub>(g) [Atomic mass of O = 16]
1 g of Li(s) [Atomic mass of Li = 7]
1 g of Ag(s) [Atomic mass of Ag = 108]
1 g of Mg(s) [Atomic mass of Mg = 24]
questions.sol:
Atoms = (mass ÷ molar mass) × atoms per formula unit × NA.

  • O₂: (1/32) × 2 = 1/16 NA
  • Li: 1/7 NA
  • Ag: 1/108 NA
  • Mg: 1/24 NA

For equal masses, the lightest atom gives the most atoms: lithium.
questions.hint: Equal masses → the smallest molar mass per atom wins. Don't forget O₂ is diatomic.

questions.q: The highest number of helium atoms is in
questions.sol:
• 4 mol → 4 NA atoms
  • 4 u is the mass of a single He atom → 1 atom
  • 4 g = 1 mol → NA atoms
  • At STP (273.15 K, 1 bar) one mole of gas occupies 22.7 L, so 2.271098 L = 0.1 mol → 0.1 NA atoms
questions.hint: u is the mass of one atom; g is the mass of one mole. At STP, 1 mol of gas = 22.7 L.

questions.q:
Among the following choose the ones with equal number of atoms.
A. 212 g of Na2CO3(s) [molar mass = 106 g]
B. 248 g of Na2O(s) [molar mass = 62 g]
C. 240 g of NaOH(s) [molar mass = 40 g]
D. 12 g of H2(g) [molar mass = 2 g]
E. 220 g of CO2(g) [molar mass = 44 g]
questions.sol:
Atoms = moles × atoms per formula unit (in units of NA):

  • A: 212/106 = 2 mol × 6 = 12
  • B: 248/62 = 4 mol × 3 = 12
  • C: 240/40 = 6 mol × 3 = 18
  • D: 12/2 = 6 mol × 2 = 12
  • E: 220/44 = 5 mol × 3 = 15

A, B and D each contain 12 NA atoms.
questions.hint: Count atoms per formula: Na₂CO₃ has 6, Na₂O 3, NaOH 3, H₂ 2, CO₂ 3.

questions.q:
The number of hydrogen atoms present in 5.4 g of urea is:
(Given: Molar mass of urea: 60 g mol−1, NA: 6.022 × 1023 particles mol−1)
questions.sol:
Urea is NH₂CONH₂: 4 H atoms per molecule.

n = 5.4 ÷ 60 = 0.09 mol → H atoms = 0.09 × 4 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.168 × 10²³.
questions.trap: Using 2 H per molecule gives 1.084 × 10²³, which is one of the options.

questions.check: NTA final answer key (Code P3): option 4
questions.q: An organic compound contains 78% (by wt.) carbon and remaining percentage of hydrogen. The right option for the empirical formula of this compound is: [Atomic wt. of C is 12, H is 1]
questions.sol:
Take 100 g: C = 78 g → 78/12 = 6.5 mol; H = 22 g → 22 mol.

Divide by the smaller: C : H = 1 : 3.38. Of the options, CH₃ (1 : 3) is the closest, and NTA's final key gives CH₃.

Note: the data do not give a clean whole-number ratio. CH₃ would need 80% carbon exactly (12/15). Pick the nearest option in the exam.
questions.hint: Assume 100 g, convert % to moles, divide by the smallest.

questions.q:
A compound X contains 32% of A, 20% of B and remaining percentage of C. Then, the empirical formula of X is:
(Given atomic masses of A = 64; B = 40; C = 32 u)
questions.sol:
C = 100 − 32 − 20 = 48%.

  • A: 32/64 = 0.5
  • B: 20/40 = 0.5
  • C: 48/32 = 1.5

Divide by 0.5 → 1 : 1 : 3, so the empirical formula is ABC₃.
questions.hint: Find % of C first, then mole ratio.

questions.q: A mixture of 2.3 g formic acid and 4.5 g oxalic acid is treated with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. The evolved gaseous mixture is passed through KOH pellets. Weight (in g) of the remaining product at STP will be
questions.sol:
Conc. H₂SO₄ removes water from both acids:

  • HCOOH → CO + H₂O: 2.3/46 = 0.05 mol → 0.05 mol CO
  • H₂C₂O₄ → CO + CO₂ + H₂O: 4.5/90 = 0.05 mol → 0.05 mol CO + 0.05 mol CO₂

KOH absorbs the CO₂. What remains is CO: 0.10 mol × 28 g mol⁻¹ = 2.8 g.
questions.hint: Write both decomposition equations; KOH removes only the acidic gas (CO₂).

questions.q: The number of moles of hydrogen molecules required to produce 20 moles of ammonia through Haber's process is:
questions.sol:
N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). Mole ratio H₂ : NH₃ = 3 : 2.

H₂ needed = 20 × 3/2 = 30 mol.
questions.hint: Read the mole ratio straight off the balanced equation.

questions.q:
The right option for the mass of CO2 produced by heating 20 g of 20% pure limestone is (Atomic mass of Ca = 40)
[CaCO3 —1200 K→ CaO + CO2]
questions.sol:
Only the pure part reacts: 20% of 20 g = 4 g CaCO₃ = 4/100 = 0.04 mol.

1 mol CaCO₃ → 1 mol CO₂, so CO₂ = 0.04 × 44 = 1.76 g.
questions.hint: Apply the purity first, then the 1 : 1 mole ratio.
questions.trap: Treating all 20 g as CaCO₃ gives 8.8 g of CO₂, which is five times too much. The impurity does not release CO₂.

questions.q: When 1 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub> gas is passed over hot coke, the volume of gaseous mixture after complete reaction at STP becomes 1.4 dm<sup>3</sup>. The composition of the gaseous mixture at STP is:
o: 0.6 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO, 0.8 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub>
0.8 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO, 0.8 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub>
0.6 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO, 0.4 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub>
0.8 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO, 0.6 dm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub>
questions.sol:
CO₂(g) + C(s) → 2CO(g). At the same T and p, gas volumes are in the same ratio as moles.

If x dm³ of CO₂ reacts, it makes 2x dm³ of CO: total = (1 − x) + 2x = 1 + x = 1.4 → x = 0.4.

CO = 0.8 dm³, CO₂ left = 0.6 dm³.
questions.hint: Coke is a solid, so only CO₂ and CO count towards the gas volume.

questions.q: 1 gram of sodium hydroxide was treated with 25 mL of 0.75 M HCl solution, the mass of sodium hydroxide left unreacted is equal to
questions.sol:
NaOH = 1/40 = 0.025 mol. HCl = 0.025 L × 0.75 M = 0.01875 mol.

NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (1 : 1), so HCl is the limiting reagent.

NaOH left = 0.025 − 0.01875 = 0.00625 mol × 40 = 0.25 g = 250 mg.
questions.hint: Moles of HCl = molarity × volume in litres; compare with moles of NaOH.

questions.check: Matches the published Code A key
questions.q: Which of the following is dependent on temperature?
questions.sol:
Molarity = moles per litre of solution. Volume expands or contracts with temperature, so molarity changes.

Molality, mole fraction and mass % use only masses or mole counts, which do not change with temperature.
questions.hint: Which term has a volume in it?

questions.q: In one molal solution that contains 0.5 mole of a solute, there is
questions.sol: Molality = moles of solute ÷ kg of solvent → 1 = 0.5 ÷ W, so W = 0.5 kg = 500 g of solvent.
questions.hint: Molality is per kg of solvent, a mass, not a volume.
questions.trap: 500 mL looks tempting, but molality never uses volume.

questions.q:
What mass of 95% pure CaCO3 will be required to neutralise 50 mL of 0.5 M HCl solution according to the following reaction?
CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + CO2(g) + H2O(l)
[Calculate upto second place of decimal point]
questions.hint: Molarity × volume → moles of HCl → halve → mass → divide by purity.
questions.trap: 1.25 g is the pure mass; forgetting the 95% purity gives that option.

questions.also: Statements C and D come from Class 12 Unit 1 (Solutions, Henry's law).
questions.q:
Identify the correct statements:
(A) The molality of 2.5 g of ethanoic acid (Molar mass: 60 g mol−1) in 75 g of benzene solution is 0.556 m.
(B) The molarity of a solution containing 5 g of NaOH (molar mass: 40 g mol−1) in 450 mL of solution is 0.278 M at 298 K.
(C) Aquatic species are more comfortable in cold water.
(D) The solubility of gas increases with decrease in pressure.
(E) For a binary mixture of A and B, the number of moles of A and B are nA and nB respectively. The mole fraction of B will be xB = nA/(nA + nB).
questions.sol:
• A ✓ 2.5/60 = 0.0417 mol ÷ 0.075 kg = 0.556 m
  • B ✓ 5/40 = 0.125 mol ÷ 0.450 L = 0.278 M
  • C ✓ Gases dissolve better at lower temperature, so cold water holds more O₂
  • D ✗ Gas solubility increases with pressure (Henry's law)
  • E ✗ xB = nB/(nA + nB); the numerator must be B's moles
questions.hint: Check A and B numerically; E is a definition check.
